--- 

Today, we're going to look at some of the practical challenges associated with
classification. Specifically, I want to hit: 

- Moving from binary to multi-class classification
- Unbalanced data
- Performance Measures

## Multi-Class Classifiers

So far, we have mainly focused on _binary_ classifiers, which distinguish between
two classes, conventionally called $\{0, 1\}$, $\{\pm 1\}$, positive/negative
*etc.* When we move to _multi-class_ classifiers-those with 3 or more (unordered)
outcomes-we have to do a bit more work. There are three broad strategies you can
consider: 

- Native multi-class: certain models can be made 'multi-class' with minimal
  additional effort. This is obviously a very nice scenario, but it does 
  restrict the models available to you. 
  
- One-vs-One: Given $K$ possible classes, train $\binom{K}{2} = \frac{K(K-1)}{2}$
  binary classifiers to compare each pair
  
- One-vs-Rest: Given $K$ possible classes, train $K$ binary classifiers to 
  predict each class vs 'something else'
  
Let's examine these each in turn. 

### Native Multi-Class

There are two broad families of models that are natively (or near natively)
suitable for multi-class classification. The first are our beloved decision
trees (and things built on top of trees, like random forests or boosting methods).
The extension here is rather straightforward: the only tweak we need is to
modify our split criterion: Rather than using binary impurity of each leaf, we 
use a multi-class modification: 

$$\text{Impurity} = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^K p_k^2$$ 

where $p_k$ is the fraction of observations in class $k$ associated with that
leaf. Here, a very pure (all one class) leaf will have $p_1 \approx 1$ and
$p_{k} \approx 0$ for all other $k$, giving an Impurity close to zero (good!).
This is essentially the same as the binary case, except we're using a sum over
$k$ probabilities. 

Alternatively, we can use a deviance (likelihood) based loss: 

$$ \text{Entropy} = -\sum_k p_k \log(p_k)$$

As before, this is small when one $p_k$ is close to 1 and the others are all
near zero. Note that this is basically the binomial deviance, but here summing
over a set of $p_k$ that add to one instead of $p$ and $1-p$. 

Other than this, multiclass decision trees work like their binary counterparts
(though some of the pre-sorting algorithmic tricks aren't quite as effective). 
Importantly, they retain their advantages of interpretability, flexibility, and
tunability (deeper vs shallow trees). 

Generative classifiers extend to multi-class problems in the obvious way. Instead
of fitting two 'reverse' models $p(X | Y=0)$ and $p(X | Y=1)$, we need $K$ models
for each $p(X | Y = k)$ and the Bayes' rule denominator is now a sum of $K$ terms,
but no other modifications are needed. (These are necessarily more 'data hungry'
but that's true of any multi-class problem.)

Finally, we can also extend logistic regression to the multi-class setting
using our general GLM machinery. While logistic regression was built on the 
_Bernoulli_ (binomial) distribution, a suitable multi-class GLM will require a
multi-class distribution. Specifically, we will build on the 
[categorical distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Categorical_distribution).[^mult]

The categorical distribution takes a set of $K$ probabilities, 
$\mathbf{p} = (p_1, p_2, \dots, p_K)$, summing to 1,
and samples according to those probabilities. A Bernoulli distribution is then
just a 2-class categorical with $\mathbf{p} = (p, 1 - p)$. The linear predictor
term is a bit more complicated: we have $K$ sets of coefficients, one for each
class. These give us $\eta_1, \dots, \eta_K$ which we then need to 'squish' into
a proper probability vector. The soft-max function to which we have made 
repeated reference is exactly the right adaptor here: 

$$\mathbf{p} = (p_1, \dots, p_K) = (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K) = (\text{softmax}(\eta_1 | \eta_1, \dots, \eta_K), \dots, \text{softmax}(\eta_K | \eta_1, \dots, \eta_K))$$

where 

$$\text{softmax}(\eta_1|\eta_1, \dots, \eta_K) = \frac{e^{\eta_1}}{\sum_{k=1}^K e^{\eta_k}}$$

You should be able to convince yourself that this is exactly the same as the 
logistic (sigmoid) link we use for ordinary logistic regression. 

While this can be built using essentially the same tools as logistic regression, 
the fitting and interpretation is a bit trickier. Specifically, note that

$$\text{softmax}(\eta_1 + c|\eta_1 + c, \dots, \eta_K + c) = \frac{e^{\eta_1 + c}}{\sum_{k=1}^K e^{\eta_k + c}} = \frac{e^{\eta_1}}{\sum_{k=1}^K e^{\eta_k}} = \text{softmax}(\eta_1|\eta_1, \dots, \eta_K)$$

so the problem is not quite well-specified. Adding a constant to all terms gives
the same prediction. To work around this, we typically add an additional 
constraint or ridge-style penalty that encourages the smallest set of coefficients
and intercept terms. 

Once the model is fit, the interpretation is a bit trickier as we now have $K$
sets of coefficients, but the general direction and sign rules are unchanged from
the binary case. 

[^mult]: You might also hear reference to the multinomial distribution in this
context. In the terminology convention I prefer, Bernoulli is to Categorical as
Binomial is to Multinomial. 

### One-vs-Rest

For models where a natively multi-class version do not exist (margin based models)
or the natively multi-class models are too finicky to work with (multinomial
regression), we can also hack together an approach based on a _set_ of 
binary classifiers.[^ens] 

Suppose we have a three way classification problem: dog *vs* cat *vs* bird. We
can build _three_ 'one-vs-rest' classifiers of the form: 

- dog *vs* not dog
- cat *vs* not cat
- bird *vs* not bird

To construct these, we essentially 'one hot encode' our response variable $Y$
and train different classifiers for each (expanded) column of the response. 
(Note that these classifiers might be quite unbalanced, a problem we'll come
back to in a bit.) After fitting these classifiers, how can we make our
predictions? Suppose we have a new test point and run it through our classifiers
and get the following probabilities: 

- dog (30%) *vs* not dog (70%)
- cat (40%) *vs* not cat (60%)
- bird (10%) *vs* not bird (90%)

How should we aggregate these to make a proper multi-class prediction? 

One approach is simply to take the most confident prediction (`cat`). This
'maximum score' strategy is simple enough, but it might feel a bit odd to
make a prediction in situations in which all probabilities are low. We can 
alternatively normalize the probabilities using the softmax transform to get

$\mathbf{p} = \frac{1}{e^{0.3} + e^{0.4} + e^{0.1}}\left(e^{0.3}, e^{0.4}, e^{0.1}\right) \approx (34\%, 38\%, 28\%)$

or a simple 'sum to one' transform. 

$\mathbf{p} = \frac{1}{0.3 + 0.4 + 0.1}\left(0.3, 0.4, 0.1\right) \approx (37.5\%, 50\%, 12.5\%)$

I am not aware of any strong argument for one transform *vs* another (and for a 
hard / point prediction they all give the same modal class) but if you are looking
at probabilitistic quality measures (like calibration), it may be worth considering
both strategies. 

This OvR strategy is rather fast (requiring only $K$ simple models) and inherits
nice properties of the binary classifiers. As we've seen, there's no guarantee
that the probabilities are meaningful and you should check calibration of the
resulting multi-way classifier, but that can usually be addressed after the fact.
More tricky is the fact that the individual classification problems can be
quite unbalanced. If you, *e.g.*, have a balanced 10-way classification problem,
each of these classifiers will be 10/90, which can cause problems for some methods.

[^ens]: While we will have many binary classifiers here, this isn't really an
_ensemble_ type of problem. We just create the different binary classifiers as 
parts from which we will build a single multi-class classifier. We aren't hoping
to aggregate them to achieve a higher level of performance.

### One-vs-One

Finally, you can also aggregate classifiers using a "one-vs-one" strategy. In
this case, we train $\binom{K}{2} = K(K-1)/2$ classifiers to compare all pairs.
For our 3-way case above, we would fit

- cat *vs* dog
- cat *vs* bird
- dog *vs* bird

(These have the same number of classifiers for $K=3$, but for $K > 3$, OvO 
requires fitting more models.) As before, we have to determine how we might 
aggregate probabilities: 


- cat (60%) *vs* dog (40%)
- cat (90%) *vs* bird (10%)
- dog (75%) *vs* bird (25%)

The simplest strategy here would be to count 'wins': 

- cat: 2 wins
- dog: 1 win
- bird: 0 wins

and to predict `cat`. This is simple enough, but it can have some real pitfalls:

1) It's not hard to come up with 'rock-paper-scissors' scenarios in which there
   is no clear winner
2) There's an 'irrelevant classifier' that gets a vote. Suppose the image was
   _actually_ a cat. Why are we letting 'dog *vs.* bird' get a say here? 
   
As $K$ gets large, this becomes particularly problematic. 

For these reasons, I don't really like the OvO strategy and rarely use it. 

### Assessing Multi-Class Accuracy

Our standard accuracy metrics (TPR, $F_1$, *etc*) derived from the $2 \times 2$
classification table do not extend as simply to the $K$-way case. OvO and OvR 
extensions of these measures exist for the multi-way case, but I find it's hard
to beat a direct examination of the classification table (confusion matrix)

## Unbalanced Classifiers

When facing real classification problems, it is not uncommon to find data sets
that are not 50/50. For instance, if you are a bank you run a fraud detector on
every credit card charge that comes over the wire. Clearly (thankfully!) the
vast majority of these are not fraudulent. But a simple accuracy metric 
can be quite useless in this setting. The 'never fraud' predictor may have
99.9% Accuracy, but zero utility. 

How should you approach this scenario? There are three broad response strategies: 

1) Use an adaptive classification threshold. In the fraud example, we might find
   that allowing a fraudulent transaction (and exposing our customers to identity
   theft) is *much* worse than forcing them to swipe twice or use a different
   card. Accounting for this, we might push our classification threshold to
   reject anything with a >3% chance of being fraud, rather than a more intuitive
   50%. 
   
Modifying the threshold can work, but it still requires a classifier that is
able to distinguish the classes (just not at the 50% point). If your classifier
isn't distinguishing classes well, this form of post-processing might not be
enough and a more direct intervention might be needed. 

2) We can modify the classification problem to upweight the rare class. Instead
   of optimizing binomial deviance (logistic regression) as an unweighted sum
   over all classes, we can put a weight $w > 1$ on the rare classes. By telling
   the optimizer that missing a fraud is 100 times worse than blocking a valid
   transaction, the model will become more aware of (and hopefully better at 
   identifying!) the rare class. Because almost all of our classifiers are defined
   by a 'sum of loss' problem, this strategy can be applied in a variety of 
   circumstances. 
   
This sort of upweighting can be quite effective, but if those rare points are
weird/noisy for whatever reason, upweighting them can induce a 'variance' penalty.
Still, keep it in mind as it is quick and powerful. 

In situations where upweighting and changing the threshold _still_ aren't enough
to get acceptable performance, we can actually go in and adjust our training
data. 

3) Modify the training data to either: 

   - randomly drop some rows of the majority class, improving balance
   - duplicate some rows of the minority class, improving balance
   - include additional synthetic rows for the minority class. (This is often
     called 'SMOTE' for ['Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_minority_oversampling_technique))
   
This is obviously the most drastic strategy we might consider as we're really
messing with the training data directly. It has some clear pitfalls you should
watch out for: 

- Dropping rows can drop signal 
- Replicating rows (or using synthetic combinations of rows) can result in data
  leakage. 
  
If you duplicate a row _before_ splitting, the same row can wind up in both
your training and your validation/test set. To avoid this, make sure to do any
data modification _within_/_inside_ of your data splitting strategy (*e.g.*, 
within each cross validation fold.)

These data modification strategies are quite dramatic, but they can be powerful
and practical, particularly for algorithms / software that isn't amenable to
observation weighting or that doesn't play well with ties. 

Finally, note that unbalanced classifiers can also occur when the data is 
collected in a non-representative way. As you saw in the previous homework, we
have far less data on rejected mortgage applications because they didn't get as
far in the underwriting process.

## Interpreting Performance Measures

When we started classification, we introduced the $2 \times 2$ classification
table and the various metrics that can be derived from it. Let's review some
of these again: 

| Metric | Formula & Plain-English Meaning | Best Used When... | Major Flaws & Blind Spots |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Accuracy** | $\frac{\text{TP} + \text{TN}}{N}$<br>*Fraction of all predictions that are correct.* | Classes are roughly balanced and false positives and false negatives carry equal cost. | **Broken under class imbalance** (predicting all negatives on 99% negative data yields 99% accuracy). Treats all mistakes as equally bad. |
| **Recall (Sensitivity / TPR)** | $\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}$<br>*Of all actual positives, what fraction did we catch?* | Missing a positive is catastrophic (e.g., cancer screening, airport security, fraud containment). | **Trivial to game:** Predicting "Positive" for every single observation achieves 100% recall while drowning users in false alarms. |
| **Precision (PPV)** | $\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}$<br>*Of all cases we flagged as positive, what fraction actually were?* | False alarms are expensive or erode user trust (e.g., spam filters, manual audit queues, automated account bans). | **Ignores missed positives:** Flagging only the single most obvious positive case in the dataset gives 100% precision while missing 99.9% of cases. |
| **Specificity (TNR)** | $\frac{\text{TN}}{\text{TN} + \text{FP}}$<br>*Of all actual negatives, what fraction did we correctly clear?* | Medical diagnostics (ruling out disease) and minimizing disruption to normal users. | Inflated when true negatives are abundant; says nothing about how many actual positives were caught. |
| **$F_1$ Score (and $F_\beta$)** | $2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$<br>*Harmonic mean of Precision and Recall.* | You need a single summary balance of catching positives and avoiding false alarms (especially on imbalanced data). | **Completely ignores True Negatives ($\text{TN}$).** Assumes Precision and Recall are equally important (unless generalized to $F_\beta$, which weights recall $\beta$ times as much as precision). |
| **Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)** | $\frac{\text{TP}\cdot\text{TN} - \text{FP}\cdot\text{FN}}{\sqrt{(\text{TP}+\text{FP})(\text{TP}+\text{FN})(\text{TN}+\text{FP})(\text{TN}+\text{FN})}}$<br>*Pearson correlation between true and predicted binary labels ($-1$ to $+1$).* | You want a single, symmetric confusion-matrix metric that rewards high performance across **all four** cells simultaneously. | Harder to explain to non-technical stakeholders than precision/recall; undefined if an entire row or column of the confusion matrix is zero. |


Beyond these scalar measures, you will also see two 'area-based' measures, the
ROC-AUC (sometimes just referred to as **the** AUC) and the PR-AUC: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels) # Includes yardstick for roc_curve() and roc_auc()


sim_preds <- tibble(
  truth = factor(rbinom(500, size = 1, prob = 0.30), levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("positive", "negative")),
  # Simulate scores with signal separation + noise
  latent_score = if_else(truth == "positive", rnorm(500, mean = 1.2, sd = 1), rnorm(500, mean = 0, sd = 1)),
  .pred_positive = plogis(latent_score)
)

auc_val <- sim_preds |>
  roc_auc(truth = truth, .pred_positive) |>
  pull(.estimate)

roc_df <- sim_preds |>
  roc_curve(truth = truth, .pred_positive)

ggplot(roc_df, aes(x = 1 - specificity, y = sensitivity)) +
  geom_path(color = "midnightblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "ROC Curve",
    subtitle = sprintf("ROC-AUC = %.3f", auc_val),
    x = "False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity)",
    y = "True Positive Rate (Sensitivity / Recall)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

For the ROC curve, we plot TPR against FPR at *every possible
threshold*. All else being equal, a curve that is more 'up and
left' will give more predictive power and will have a larger
area under the curve. This is a useful technique for getting
an overall picture, but it does not necessarily give proper 
guidance _at a particular threshold_. 

An alternative to the ROC is the PR curve which plots
precision against recall. 

```{r}
#| echo: false

pr_auc_val <- sim_preds |>
  pr_auc(truth = truth, .pred_positive) |>
  pull(.estimate)

pr_df <- sim_preds |>
  pr_curve(truth = truth, .pred_positive)

# Positive class prevalence (the random-classifier baseline for PR curves)
pos_baseline <- mean(sim_preds$truth == "positive")

ggplot(pr_df, aes(x = recall, y = precision)) +
  geom_path(color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pos_baseline, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Precision–Recall Curve",
    subtitle = sprintf("PR-AUC = %.3f | Random Baseline = %.2f", pr_auc_val, pos_baseline),
    x = "Recall (Sensitivity)",
    y = "Precision (Positive Predictive Value)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Note that the 'baseline' here is based on the positive prevalance (*i.e.*, the 'prior' or fixed/null model probability), not a 
straight 50/50 tradeoff. 

As with ROC-AUC, this gives a nice summary picture, but it may not
be determinative at a single threshold value.
